title: Bangkok in 5 Days — Grand Palace, Wat Arun, Chatuchak, ICONSIAM
subtitle: The Grand Palace, Wat Arun, Chatuchak Weekend Market and ICONSIAM
summary: Five days in Bangkok: day 1 is the airport arrival plus a hotel sky bar, followed by the Grand Palace, Wat Arun, Chatuchak, ICONSIAM and Jodd Fairs night market, and the last morning is a park before you fly out. Chatuchak needs a weekend. The notes cover the TDAC arrival card, getting between the airport and the city, transit cards, internet and cash. Chinatown, Old Siam and Central Rama 9 are in the alternates.

Changes and trade-offs

The travelogue originally covered 5 days including the travel days; this version turns day 1 into the airport arrival plus a hotel sky bar, and leaves only a morning park visit and the departure on day 5.
The travelogue's breakfasts (Wang Chunsheng beef hotpot and the hotel breakfast) are left out; promotional links are removed and only official links remain.
Entry

Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC): every foreign visitor must fill it in free on the official site https://tdac.immigration.go.th and submit it within 3 days before arrival (including the day of arrival); you must refile on every entry. Use only the official site — any site that charges is fake.
Between the airport and the city

Airport Rail Link: from Suvarnabhumi to Phaya Thai takes about 26–30 minutes and costs THB 15–45, with the airport to Phaya Thai about THB 45; it runs from about 05:30 to midnight, every 10–15 minutes. Only single-journey tickets are sold, and the Rabbit Card is not accepted.

The 2024 travelogue's route: Airport Rail Link to Phaya Thai, the BTS Sukhumvit Line to Siam, then the BTS Silom Line to Chong Nonsi; after the exit, walk across the skywalk and then about 15 minutes to the hotel; at night the lights are few and walking alone is frightening.

Taxi: public taxis queue on the ground floor (Public Taxi) and charge by the meter plus the THB 50 airport service charge, with the expressway toll of about THB 70–80 paid separately; to the city usually about THB 400–575; Grab also works, and the travelogue's return from the hotel to the airport was THB 577 including tolls.
Before the taxi reaches the hotel the road is a two-way street, so the driver has to overshoot and make a U-turn, adding a short detour.
Transport cards
At the BTS staffed windows you can buy a Rabbit Card, top it up and tap in and out; the Rabbit Card works only on the BTS, not on the MRT or the Airport Rail Link.
For the MRT buy a ticket, or tap in and out directly with a VISA contactless card (this worked in the travelogue's test; check yourself whether your bank supports it).
Before you leave Taiwan, register for Grab and link a credit card.
The Chao Phraya piers have official ticket counters; do not take the private boats touting outside the pier.
Internet and cash
The travelogue used an eSIM (AIS); activating it needs an internet connection, so it is best to activate it in Taiwan first; the airport has free Wi-Fi.

Changing baht: the travelogue changed money at SuperRich in The Old Siam Shopping Plaza near Wat Pho; banknotes must not be stained or written on, and SuperRich keeps hours, so you cannot change if you arrive too early or too late.
Bookings
The Rock Pub: on the travelogue's night the ticket was THB 350 with one drink, bought in advance.
King Power Mahanakhon: tickets bought online are usually cheaper than at the door; confirm the daytime or sunset session first.
Zoom Sky Bar: if you want dinner, book ahead — arriving late may leave only bar snacks.
Lodging

4 nights in Sathorn: the travelogue stayed at JC Kevin Sathorn Bangkok Hotel, an apartment-style suite about 1 kilometer, or 15 minutes on foot, from Chong Nonsi BTS Station. The travelogue booked late and paid a high price; booking early can be much cheaper.
Weather and season
The travelogue visited in August, when afternoon thunderstorms are common, so schedule temple visits in the morning.

Chatuchak Weekend Market is fully open only on Saturday and Sunday. This template puts it on day 3, so when you apply dates make day 3 a Saturday or Sunday; otherwise swap it with day 4 and go somewhere else.
Thai limits on alcohol sales: 11:00–14:00 and 17:00–24:00, and no alcohol is sold all day on Buddhist holidays (travelogue data).
Dress and safety
The Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun all have dress codes: no shorts, bare shoulders, ripped jeans, cropped trousers or short skirts.
Beware of pickpockets in crowds; anyone outside an attraction who says it is closed and steers you to a tuk-tuk or a private boat is running a scam.
The travelogue met a scam in which a stranger starts a conversation to swap money and look at banknotes; ignore it.
The emergency line for foreigners is 1155.
Tipping is not part of Thai culture; for a massage the travelogue gave THB 20 as a token.
Other
A reminder from the travelogue: mango sticky rice cannot be brought back to Taiwan.
Alternates: The Old Siam Shopping Plaza in the old town, Chinatown (Yaowarat Road) and Central Rama 9 are kept as alternate sights.
